newsitem.title: THAILAND: Hopes of Thai rebound boost S.E. currencies.
newsitem.headline: Hopes of Thai rebound boost S.E. currencies.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies rose on Tuesday to levels not seen for a week as optimism about an impending rescue package for Thailand's woebegone economy spread through the region.
Dealers said the Thai government's decision to seek help from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Japan's endorsement of the move helped restore confidence that the economy would rise again.
"All this is pointing to a recovery. It may take a while, but everything's looking more positive," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore.
She said the entire regional currency market was being driven by renewed hopes about Thailand. "There's the idea that we've seen the worst and it's set to improve now."
The market was undeterred by news of Thai central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond's resignation.
It had been expected for some time and some players even viewed Rerngchai's departure as a positive development, blaming him for Thailand's economic crisis.
"On the baht spot market, it looks like people are taking the Thai governor's resignation as a good sign," one dealer said.
The Thai baht was at 31.00/40 to the dollar onshore at 0415 GMT after firming to 30.45 against 31.90-32.00 late on Monday. It was at 30.95/31.05 in offshore markets.
Dealers said the baht's rise was accelerated by relatively thin trading volumes, but it was expected to face some resistance around the 30 level.
"The baht has been trading very strong since they announced this (IMF news). But Thailand still needs lower interest rates so dollar/baht will not have much room on the downside," a dealer said.

In Malaysia, the ringgit benefited from the baht's recovery and continued nervousness about the possible imposition of capital controls after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's veiled threats on Monday.
Mahathir's comment about unspecified punitive actions against currency speculators triggered a selloff in dollar/ringgit, pushing it down 300 points.

Dealers said stop-loss dollar sales and thin volumes added to the ringgit's gains. They said it was likely to benefit in the near term from month-end demand and continued uncertainty over possible curbs.

The Singapore dollar extended its rise, firming through the key 1.46 to the U.S. dollar level after breaching 1.47 in Monday afternoon trade. Dealers said the Singapore dollar was likely to face near-term resistance around 1.4575.
The Indonesian rupiah rose on offshore dollar sales but dealers said domestic dollar demand was blocking further rises around the 2,550 level.
"I think we may see attempts to break the 2,550 level as regional markets recover," a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said.
However, dealers said overnight dollars were expensive, with trades ranging around 11.0/12.0 percent.

The Philippine central bank sold dollars at 28.48 pesos in early trade to counter continued dollar demand from importers, traders said. The peso was quoted at 28.48/53 at 0415 GMT against its previous close at 28.479.
The Taiwan dollar caved in to weeks of pressure, falling through a key support of T$28 in early trade as the central bank dropped its defence of that level, Taipei dealers said.
It was at T$28.165/169 at 0415 GMT against Monday's T$27.972 close but dealers said the rate was stabilising and was unlikely to tumble further.
They said recent pressure on the Taiwan dollar stemmed from the U.S. dollar's rally against major currencies and from some speculative attacks in the form of non-delivery forward trading.
